title: China's Diplomatic Balancing Act: Can It Mediate Between Iran and the U.S.?
summary:
As tensions escalate between Iran and the United States, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi is expected in Beijing on Wednesday for his second visit to the Chinese capital since the U.S.-Israel war on Iran began at the end of February. He will meet with his Chinese counterpart, Wang Yi. The trip comes shortly before a planned meeting between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington later in September.

The timing highlights China's attempt to frame itself as a neutral party seeking an end to the conflict. At a BRICS summit in New Delhi this week, Xi urged the bloc of Global South powers to act as peacemakers in the Middle East and said China was willing to work with them. He promoted a broad four-point plan for de-escalation centered on peaceful coexistence, respect for national sovereignty, adherence to international law, and balancing development and security.

However, analysts caution that China has traditionally avoided deeply entangling itself in third-party conflicts and potentially failed diplomatic initiatives. Hamed Vafaei, a professor at the University of Tehran, said perceiving Xi's remarks as an offer to mediate between Iran and the U.S. was more of a "free interpretation" than reality.

Araghchi is also expected to discuss Iran's nuclear program. Last week, the U.S. and its European allies successfully pushed the board of the UN nuclear watchdog, the IAEA, to refer Iran to the UN Security Council. The last such referral came 20 years ago and was followed by six UN Security Council resolutions and sweeping sanctions. This time, the move is expected to be largely symbolic because China and Russia can veto any new Security Council measures.

Western pressure continues elsewhere. Iran's nuclear chief Mohammad Eslami was barred from attending this week's IAEA General Conference in Vienna under "snapback" sanctions reimposed by European powers last year. The U.S. has launched "Operation Economic Outcast" to further isolate Iran, including a naval blockade of its southern ports. China remains the largest buyer of Iranian crude oil and has vowed to protect its interests despite the sanctions.
why_it_matters: Whether China can act as a genuine mediator — or mainly as a buyer of Iranian oil with its own interests — will shape how dangerous the Middle East standoff becomes and shows how far global power has shifted away from a single superpower.

background_read: The IAEA (the International Atomic Energy Agency) is the United Nations' nuclear watchdog, based in Vienna; it inspects nuclear sites and reports concerns to the UN Security Council, which has 15 members — but five of them (the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France) hold permanent seats and can veto any resolution.

In 2015, Iran signed a nuclear deal with world powers that limited its uranium enrichment in exchange for relief from sanctions; the United States left that deal in 2018 and reimposed sanctions, and Iran has since expanded its nuclear work.
A 'snapback' is a mechanism built into that original deal that allows participants to restore UN sanctions without the usual Security Council vote, which is why European powers were able to use it.

BRICS — originally Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa — is a bloc of mostly Global South economies that has recently expanded and often presents itself as an alternative to Western-led groupings such as the G7.
Wang Yi is China's foreign minister and Xi Jinping has been China's president since 2013; China is also the largest buyer of Iranian crude oil, which complicates its claim to be a neutral mediator.

perspectives.description: Beijing gains a chance to look like a global peacemaker rather than a bystander, and BRICS members get a platform to argue that the Global South should broker its own deals. Iran, meanwhile, keeps a powerful customer for its oil and a diplomatic channel to Washington's rivals.

Sceptics note that China has historically avoided deep involvement in other countries' conflicts and failed initiatives, and that its neutrality is questionable when it is the biggest buyer of sanctioned Iranian crude. Hamed Vafaei of the University of Tehran calls the idea of Chinese mediation a 'free interpretation' rather than reality.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral / analytical — the tools being used
perspectives.description: The IAEA referral echoes the pattern of 20 years ago, when a similar move was followed by six Security Council resolutions and sweeping sanctions. This time the mechanics are different: because permanent members can veto, the referral works more as political pressure than as a path to binding new measures.

The planned Trump–Xi meeting in Washington will test whether Beijing's diplomacy produces real talks or just positioning before the encounter. At the same time, snapback sanctions and the U.S. naval blockade keep raising the cost for Iran, which could push it either to negotiate or to escalate.
